Visualizing The Buying Power Of The U.S. Dollar Over The Last Century
Put another way, since 1913, the "dollar" now actually the federal reserve note, has lost over 97% of its value.

The value of money is not static.

And there's the problem. The value of money should be static. If it was managed properly, it could be static. Not in terms of goods, because technology and resource availability changes the intrinsic value of goods. We call that changes in productivity.

The value of money needs to be in something that does not change. The thing that does not change is the same unit that the universe uses to measure value, energy. So, if we set the value of money at 1 Kilowatt or 1 Megawatt, then it is always the same. It is then merely an exercise in determining how much of the energy spent in the economy went to productive uses and how much was consumed to set the amount of money that the economy produced. In other words, bookkeeping; complicated bookkeeping, but bookkeeping.

Then there is no inflation, there is only an ongoing conflict between lowered energy cost because of innovation and increased energy cost because of resource exhaustion.

Note that this says nothing about the prices that are set - they are still determined by supply and demand. And if the price of a good in energy is less than the cost of the good in energy, it stops being produced.
